sections.content: The chapter introduces the Vaikhānasas as a community of temple-priests, ordained by birth to worship Viṣṇu. They are enjoined to follow no other profession and eke out their livelihood as priests. They adhere strictly to the rites prescribed in the Vaikhānasa-sūtra and Śāstra. Their practices are a combination of Vedic fire-rituals and Āgama iconic worship. They undergo eighteen sacramental rites (saṁskāras) and perform twenty-six yajñas. They call themselves 'vaidikas' due to their acceptance of the ultimate authority of the Vedas and the use of Vedic mantras in all rituals. The section introduces Śrīnivāsa-makhin's Daśa-vidha-hetu-nirūpaṇam (c. 1050 A.D.) as a key text outlining their characteristic features.
sections.summary: This section defines the Vaikhānasa community as hereditary temple-priests dedicated to Viṣṇu worship. It highlights their unique blend of Vedic and Āgamic traditions, adherence to their specific sūtras, and self-identification as 'vaidikas'.

sections.content: This section details ten characteristic features of the Vaikhānasa scriptures, as outlined in Śrīnivāsa-makhin's work. These points establish the authority, antiquity, and unique nature of their tradition: (1) The scriptures are given by Vikhanas (Brahmā). (2) They are the earliest of the sūtras, belonging to the Taittirīya branch of Kṛṣṇa-yajurveda. (3) They strictly follow Vedic authority in all rituals. (4) All rites are invariably accompanied by Vedic mantras. (5) All sacramental rites (saṁskāras) from conception to death are conducted according to Vedic injunctions. (6) They insist on the purification of the individual through eighteen bodily rites. (7) The Vaikhānasa-kalpa-sūtra is self-contained and complete. (8) Its style and content have been accepted by other law-givers like Manu. (9) The scriptures are exclusively devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. (10) Viṣṇu himself has declared that followers of this sūtra are dearest to him, citing a verse from the Varāha-purāṇa.
sections.summary: This part enumerates ten defining principles of the Vaikhānasa tradition that assert its divine origin from Brahmā (Vikhanas), its primacy among sūtra literature, its unwavering adherence to Vedic authority and mantras, its comprehensive ritual framework, its exclusive focus on Viṣṇu, and its favored status by Viṣṇu himself.

sections.content: This section explores the origins of the name 'Vikhanas'. The community traces its descent from the sage Vikhanas, a name that can refer to Brahmā or even Viṣṇu himself. The root 'khanana' (to dig) is central to several etymological explanations. One view is that Brahmā was called Vikhanas because he 'dug' into his own mind ('manasaḥ khananāt') to create the scriptural lore. Another, from the Mahābhārata, is that he 'dug' into his own heart through penance. The Ānanda-samhitā suggests Viṣṇu became Vikhanas by 'digging up' the essential meaning of the Upaniṣads. The Nṛsiṁha-purāṇa distinguishes between an 'older' Brahmā (Vikhanas, author of the sūtras) born from Viṣṇu's mind, and a 'younger' four-faced Brahmā born from Viṣṇu's navel for creation. An alternative meaning is derived from 'vi-nakha', meaning one with tranquil sense-organs. The section concludes that 'Vikhanas' has multiple meanings, including Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the progenitor sage, and the author of the sūtras, all of which contribute to the community's identity.
sections.summary: The name 'Vikhanas' is deeply significant and multi-layered. It is primarily derived from the act of 'digging' for profound knowledge, whether by Brahmā into his mind, Viṣṇu into the Vedas, or a sage into the heart through penance. The term can refer to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or the primordial sage, establishing a divine lineage for the Vaikhānasa community.

sections.section_title: Origin Stories of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra and Community
sections.content: Several narratives explaining the origin of the Vaikhānasa scriptures and community are presented. According to Atri, Viṣṇu initially taught Brahmā a vast worship manual that was later lost. Brahmā, through severe austerities in the Naimiśa forest, re-perceived this knowledge and became known as Vikhanas. He then abridged it and taught it to his four hermit sons—Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, and Kāśyapa—who became known as Vaikhānasas and were responsible for forming the community. Bhṛgu's Prakīrṇādhikāra offers another account where Brahmā forgot the Vedas after slumber and recovered them by worshipping Viṣṇu, earning the name Vikhanas. He then taught this wisdom to ten mind-born seers. Kriyādhikāra narrates how Viṣṇu repeatedly recovered the Vedas for Brahmā from demons, establishing the Vaikhānasa (Vedic) mode of worship as supreme over Tāntrik methods used in the Vedas' absence. Finally, an account from Ānanda-samhitā describes the sage Vikhanas being instructed by Nara-Nārāyaṇa at Badarī to spread iconic worship, leading him to teach nine sages in the Naimiśa forest.
sections.summary: This section compiles various mythological accounts of the Vaikhānasa tradition's origins. Common themes include the loss and divine recovery of sacred knowledge (the Vedas or the Sūtra itself) by Brahmā (as Vikhanas) through the grace of Viṣṇu, followed by the transmission of this knowledge to a group of primary sages (typically four or nine) who founded the community.

sections.section_title: The Concept of 'Garbha-Vaiṣṇava' and Distinction from Other Priests
sections.content: This part details the core Vaikhānasa belief of being Viṣṇu-devotees by birth ('garbha-vaiṣṇava-janmanām'), which sets them apart from other communities. This status is conferred through a unique sacrament called Viṣṇu-bali (or garbhacakra saṁskāra), performed during the eighth month of pregnancy. The ritual is believed to bestow upon the unborn child the status of a Vaiṣṇava, with Viṣṇu himself branding the foetus with the marks of his conch and discus. This pre-natal initiation means a Vaikhānasa is born sanctified and requires no further initiatory rites (dīkṣā) to become a priest. This is contrasted with the Pāñcarātra tradition, which employs a post-natal branding ceremony (tapta-mudrāṅkana). Vaikhānasas are strictly forbidden from undergoing this external ritual. The text also distinguishes them from 'devalakas', or professional priests who worship for monetary gain. A Vaikhānasa is expected to worship out of devotion and duty, not as a profession for livelihood, making their priesthood an inherent part of their being rather than a career.
sections.summary: Vaikhānasas are considered 'Vaiṣṇavas from the womb' (Garbha-Vaiṣṇava) due to a unique prenatal sacrament, Viṣṇu-bali. This inherent sanctity eliminates the need for post-birth initiations like the branding rituals found in Pāñcarātra. They also distinguish themselves from 'devalakas' by asserting that their priesthood is a lifelong, devotional duty, not a profession for financial reward.

sections.section_title: Vaikhānasa Viewpoint on Worship and the Deity
sections.content: This section explains the Vaikhānasa philosophy of worship. While recognized as a Śrī-Vaiṣṇava sect, they do not follow Rāmānujācārya or the Āḻvārs, and their worship is conducted entirely with Vedic hymns, devoid of Tāntrik elements like seed-syllables (bījākṣara). They acknowledge both formless (nirākāra) and formal (sākāra) worship, but consider iconic worship (arcā) more significant. For them, a consecrated icon is not merely symbolic but a real manifestation of the divine, with God's presence abiding in it permanently after installation (pratiṣṭhā). This formal worship is an expedient for the human mind to eventually grasp the formless Absolute. A key aspect shared with Tāntrik tradition is the identification of the worshipper with the deity. The priest recites the 'Ātma-sūkta' to achieve a state of meditative absorption, becoming one with Viṣṇu before transferring this divinity to the icon. This leads to the concept of the priest as a 'mobile god'.
sections.summary: The Vaikhānasa worship is purely Vedic, rejecting Tāntrik practices and the authority of later Śrī-Vaiṣṇava saints. They view consecrated icons as real divine manifestations, essential for leading the devotee toward the formless Absolute. A unique feature is the priest's ritual identification with Viṣṇu through the recitation of the Ātma-sūkta, making the priest himself a sacred vessel of divinity.

sections.content: The 'Ātma-sūkta' is a collection of nine verses in the triṣṭubh metre, unique to Vaikhānasa worship. It is recited to invoke Viṣṇu's cosmic (sa-kala) form. The hymn's purpose is to transform the individual self of the priest into the cosmic spirit, allowing his constitution to accommodate Viṣṇu's vast form. The verses systematically identify the priest's self, breaths, bodily functions, and physical parts with the supreme self, cosmic deities (Varāha, Hayagrīva), natural elements (mountains, rivers), Vedic lore, and the sages (Bhṛgu). The hymn culminates with Viṣṇu entering the priest's 'pure lotus of the heart' and the priest becoming a personification of all gods, sages, and merit.
sections.summary: This section presents the full text and translation of the Ātma-sūkta, a key hymn in Vaikhānasa ritual. Through this hymn, the priest ritually transforms his individual body and consciousness into a microcosm of the cosmos, identifying with divine forces and creating a vessel suitable for invoking and becoming one with the cosmic form of Viṣṇu.

sections.section_title: The Mūrti System and Aspects of Godhead
sections.content: This section discusses the Vaikhānasa system of multiple icons and the corresponding aspects of Godhead. Temple worship involves a main, immoveable stone icon (dhruva-bimba) and several moveable icons that represent Viṣṇu's 'three strides'. These are the kautuka-bera (for daily worship), snapana-bera (for rituals), and utsava-bera (for processions). A fifth, bali-bera, may be added. These are not independent deities but emanations of the dhruva-bimba. Analogous to this is the conception of Godhead's aspects. The Vaikhānasa system identifies five forms: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha. This is distinct from the Pāñcarātra four-fold vyūha (Vāsudeva, etc.). These five aspects are linked to the four stages of emancipation (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya), each occurring in a specific plane of Viṣṇu's sphere (Āmoda, Pramoda, etc.) and presided over by an aspect of the Godhead. In temple worship, these four aspects are visualized around Viṣṇu and correspond to the different icons, creating a cohesive ritual and theological system.
sections.summary: Vaikhānasa temple practice is structured around a system of multiple icons (catur-mūrti/pañca-mūrti), where moveable icons are emanations of the main immoveable one. This physical arrangement mirrors a theological system of Godhead's five aspects (Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha), which are in turn linked to the progressive stages of spiritual emancipation.

sections.section_title: Idealistic Outlook and the Role of Icons
sections.content: The chapter concludes by emphasizing that despite the elaborate system of iconic forms (bera), consorts (devī), and divine retinues (parivāra), the Vaikhānasa outlook is fundamentally idealistic. Godhead is ultimately held to be inscrutable, immutable, indefinable, and without qualities (nirguṇa). He pervades everything like butter in milk or fire in wood. The absolute must be conjured in the mind and invoked within the heart. The tangible, cosmic form (sa-kala) of Viṣṇu that is worshipped is understood as the absolute materializing itself through the devotee's devotion and visualization. The text credits Śaunaka with counseling that worshipping a beautiful, delightful icon of Viṣṇu facilitates contemplation, allowing the devotee to ultimately merge with that very form of Brahman.
sections.summary: This final section reconciles the detailed ritualism of Vaikhānasa worship with its idealistic philosophy. The worship of forms and icons is not an end in itself but a necessary and effective means (an expedient) to facilitate the contemplation of an otherwise inscrutable, formless Absolute (Brahman), ultimately leading to union with it.
key_concepts: Icon as a tool for contemplation

chapter_summary: Chapter II provides a comprehensive overview of the Vaikhānasa community, detailing their identity, scriptures, origins, and unique theological and ritualistic viewpoints. They are defined as a hereditary caste of temple-priests devoted exclusively to the worship of Viṣṇu, blending Vedic fire-rituals with Āgamic iconic worship. The chapter traces their lineage to the sage Vikhanas (identified with Brahmā or Viṣṇu), whose name derives from 'digging' for profound knowledge. A central tenet is the concept of 'Garbha-Vaiṣṇava', where members are considered initiated from the womb via a special prenatal rite, distinguishing them from the Pāñcarātra tradition and its post-birth branding rituals. The Vaikhānasa worldview is staunchly Vedic, rejecting Tāntrik elements and later Śrī-Vaiṣṇava developments. Their worship revolves around a sophisticated system of multiple icons (catur-mūrti) that correspond to aspects of Godhead and stages of emancipation. A key ritual is the recitation of the Ātma-sūkta, where the priest identifies with the cosmic form of Viṣṇu. Ultimately, the chapter argues that despite the focus on elaborate iconic worship, the Vaikhānasa outlook is idealistic, viewing the icon as an essential expedient for the devotee to contemplate and ultimately realize the formless, all-pervading Brahman.
key_arguments: The Vaikhānasa community's identity is rooted in being priests by birth, a status conferred through a unique prenatal sacrament (Viṣṇu-bali).
Vaikhānasa scriptures and rituals are of divine origin (from Vikhanas/Brahmā) and represent the most ancient and authentic Vedic form of Viṣṇu worship.
The Vaikhānasa tradition is distinct from and superior to the Tāntra-based Pāñcarātra tradition, particularly in its rejection of external initiations like branding.
Iconic worship in the Vaikhānasa system is not merely symbolic; the icon is a real manifestation of the divine, serving as a necessary aid for contemplating the formless Absolute.
The priest plays a central role, becoming a 'mobile god' through ritual identification with Viṣṇu via the Ātma-sūkta.
key_takeaways: Vaikhānasas are a unique, conservative sect of Vaiṣṇava priests who claim direct descent from a primordial sage and adherence to the original Vedic form of worship.
Their concept of being 'Vaiṣṇavas from the womb' (Garbha-Vaiṣṇava) is a cornerstone of their identity and distinguishes them from other Vaiṣṇava groups.
The elaborate system of multiple icons (catur-mūrti) in their temples is deeply symbolic, representing both the pervasive nature of Viṣṇu and the devotee's path to liberation.
The Ātma-sūkta is a specific and powerful hymn that facilitates the priest's temporary transformation into the cosmic deity, which is central to their invocation ritual.
The Vaikhānasa tradition successfully integrates a highly detailed, form-based (sākāra) ritual practice with an ultimate philosophical goal of realizing the formless (nirākāra) Brahman.

historical_figures.name: Śrīnivāsa-makhin
historical_figures.significance: Authored 'Daśa-vidha-hetu-nirūpaṇam' and 'Tātparya-cintāmaṇi', which are cited as authoritative texts explaining the Vaikhānasa viewpoint.

historical_figures.name: Vikhanas
historical_figures.significance: The divine ancestor of the Vaikhānasa community and author of their foundational scripture, the Vaikhānasa-sūtra. Variously identified with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or a mind-born sage.

historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
historical_figures.significance: The central object of worship for the Vaikhānasa community. He is also described as the ultimate source of their scriptural knowledge and in some accounts is identified with Vikhanas himself.

historical_figures.name: Brahmā
historical_figures.significance: Frequently identified with the sage Vikhanas, who received the divine knowledge from Viṣṇu and authored the sūtras.

historical_figures.name: Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Kāśyapa
historical_figures.significance: The four hermit sons or disciples of Vikhanas who received the Vaikhānasa teachings and are credited with codifying them and founding the community. They are also considered authors of major Vaikhānasa texts.

historical_figures.name: Manu
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the other sūtra-writers who accepted the contents and style of the Vaikhānasa-kalpa-sūtra.

historical_figures.name: Nara and Nārāyaṇa
historical_figures.significance: In one origin story, they instructed the sage Vikhanas at Badarī to enlighten mankind about iconic worship.

historical_figures.name: Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu
historical_figures.significance: Listed alongside the main four sages as disciples of Vikhanas in the Naimiśa forest.

historical_figures.name: Nṛsimha-Vājapeya-yāji
historical_figures.significance: Cited as the source for details on the worship of Vikhanas and the Viṣṇu-bali ceremony.

historical_figures.name: Hārīta
historical_figures.significance: His view is cited to distinguish Vaikhānasas from professional priests (devalakas).

historical_figures.name: Rāmānujācārya
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a guru whom the Vaikhānasas, unlike other Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas, do not recognize.

historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as guides whose hymns (Prabandha) are not recited in Vaikhānasa worship.

historical_figures.name: Śaunaka
historical_figures.significance: Credited with the counsel to worship a beautiful icon of Viṣṇu to facilitate contemplation and attain Brahman.

historical_figures.name: Yudhiṣṭhira and Kṛṣṇa
historical_figures.significance: Their dialogue in the Mahābhārata is cited to explain the Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra views on the forms of Godhead.

historical_events.significance: Provides a systematic account of the characteristic features and authority of the Vaikhānasa scriptures.

geographic_locations.context: A sacred forest where Brahmā (as Vikhanas) performed austerities to recover lost divine knowledge, and where Vikhanas taught the foundational scriptures to his sage-disciples.
geographic_locations.significance: It serves as the mythological location for the origin and propagation of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra.

geographic_locations.context: A location where the sage Vikhanas performed austerities before traveling to the Himalayas.
geographic_locations.significance: A place of spiritual preparation for the sage Vikhanas.

geographic_locations.context: A site in the Himalayas where Vikhanas met the divine sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa and was instructed by them to spread the knowledge of iconic worship.
geographic_locations.significance: The location where the mission to disseminate Vaikhānasa teachings was divinely ordained.

quotations.quote: अश्वत्त्थः कपिला गावः तुलसी विखना मुनिः । चत्वारो मत्प्रिया राजन् तेषां वैखानसो वरः ॥
quotations.context: A verse where Viṣṇu declares four things are dear to him, with the sage Vikhanas being the dearest.

quotations.quote: आदिकाले तु भगवान् ब्रह्मा तु विखना मुनिः। यजुः शाखानुसारेण चक्रे सूत्रं महत्तरम्।
quotations.context: States that the sage Vikhanas who prepared the Vaikhānasa-sūtra was Brahmā himself.

quotations.quote: विखना वै विष्णुः तज्जा वैखानसा स्मृताः।
quotations.context: Identifies Vikhanas with Viṣṇu, and Vaikhānasas as his offspring.

quotations.quote: नारायणः पिता यस्य माता हरिप्रिया। भृग्वादिमुनयः शिष्यास्तस्मै विखनसे नमः ॥
quotations.context: A prayer describing Vikhanas as having Viṣṇu for a father, Lakṣmī for a mother, and sages like Bhṛgu as disciples.

quotations.quote: त्वत्सुतो भाग्यवान् धन्यो गर्भवैष्णवसंज्ञितः । अप्राकृतो महात्मासौ गर्भचक्रेण लांछितः ॥
quotations.context: Mantra recited during the Viṣṇu-bali ceremony, declaring the unborn child a 'garbha-vaiṣṇava'.

quotations.quote: श्री वैखानससूत्रस्थस्तप्तमुद्रो भवेद्यदि । आलयं न विशेत्पश्चात् पूजनं नैव कारयेत्।
quotations.context: Prohibiting a Vaikhānasa who has undergone branding (tapta-mudrā) from entering the temple or performing worship.

quotations.quote: वैष्णवं द्विविधं शास्त्रं मुनिभिः परिकीर्त्तितम् । वैखानसं वैदिकं स्याद्वैदिकैरर्चितं द्विजैः ॥
quotations.context: Distinguishing between the two kinds of Vaiṣṇava scripture: Vaikhānasa (Vedic) and Pāñcarātra (Tantrik).

quotations.quote: रूपद्वयं हरेः प्रोक्त बिम्बमर्चक एव च। बिम्बं त्वावाहनादूध्व सदा सन्निहितोऽर्चक ॥ अर्चकस्तु हरिः साक्षाच्चर रूपी न संशयः ।
quotations.context: Stating that Viṣṇu has two forms: the icon (bimba) and the priest (arcaka), and that the priest is a mobile, living form of Hari (Viṣṇu).

quotations.quote: आत्मात्मा परमान्तरात्मा मह्यन्तरात्म। यश्चादिरात्मा स तु नोन्तरात्मा । व्यावेष्टि विश्वं सकलं बिभर्ति । यो व्यक्तपुण्यः स तु नः प्रधानः ॥१॥
quotations.context: The first verse of the Ātma-sūkta, identifying the individual self with the supreme self.
Defining the Vaikhānasa mode of worship as that which is done with Vedic hymns.

quotations.quote: विष्णुश्चैव महाविष्णुः सदाविष्णुरिति क्रमात् ॥ व्यापी नारायण इति तन्नामानि ततः क्रमात् ॥
quotations.context: Listing the names of the presiding deities for the four stages of emancipation: Viṣṇu, Mahā-viṣṇu, Sadā-viṣṇu, and Vyāpī-nārāyaṇa.

controversial_points: The Vaikhānasa claim of being the earliest and most authentic Vedic tradition of Viṣṇu worship, positioning the Pāñcarātra tradition as a later, non-Vedic (Tantrik) development.
The absolute prohibition of the Pāñcarātra initiation rite of branding (tapta-mudrāṅkana) for Vaikhānasas, with severe consequences of disqualification from priesthood for those who undergo it.

The text's refutation of the Mahābhārata's claim that the Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra theological viewpoints on the forms of Godhead are the same ('anarthāntara'), stating this is 'rather hard to substantiate'.
alternative_viewpoints: The Pāñcarātra tradition's use of initiatory rites like 'tapta-mudrāṅkana' is presented as an alternative to the Vaikhānasa concept of being initiated by birth.
The Pāñcarātra theological system of four vyūhas (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) is contrasted with the Vaikhānasa system of five forms (Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha).
